stem: Which combination of findings places a hospitalized client at increased risk for pressure injury?

options.A: Full mobility, intact sensation, adequate nutrition, and dry skin.
options.B: Independent repositioning, intact sensation, and adequate nutritional intake.
options.C: Frequent ambulation, intact sensory perception, and no moisture exposure.
options.D: Limited mobility, impaired sensory perception, poor nutrition, and persistent moisture exposure.

rationale: Current NCBI guidance identifies decreased mobility, moisture, poor nutritional status, and loss of sensory perception among the major pressure-injury risk factors. These same domains are included in the Braden risk assessment framework. D is correct.
educational_objective: Recognize major patient factors that increase pressure-injury risk.
source_organization: National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI), StatPearls
source_locator: Etiology; History and Physical; Evaluation — Braden Scale
source_claim_supported: Common pressure-injury risk factors include decreased mobility, moisture, poor nutritional status, and loss of sensory perception; Braden assesses sensory perception, moisture, activity, mobility, nutrition, and friction/shear.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Reduction of Risk Potential — identify risk factors and prevent complications
blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — pressure-injury risk assessment

source_original.stem: A nurse is identifying risk factors for pressure injury development in a hospitalized client. Which factor would place a client at increased risk?

options.A: Excellent nutritional status with adequate protein intake and no other identifiable pressure injury risk factors present
options.B: Ability to independently reposition every couple of hours without requiring staff assistance or reminders
options.C: Full mobility with an independent repositioning ability and no reported sensory or nutritional impairment
options.D: Immobility, impaired sensory perception, poor nutrition, and excessive moisture (such as from incontinence)

source_original.rationale: Key risk factors for pressure injury development include immobility (inability to independently reposition), impaired sensory perception (reduced ability to feel and respond to pressure/discomfort), poor nutritional status, and excessive moisture (such as from incontinence), all of which are assessed as part of tools like the Braden Scale to guide individualized prevention strategies.
source_original.source_detail: AHRQ Pressure Injury Prevention, Braden risk dimensions: sensory perception, moisture, activity, mobility, nutrition, friction/shear; accessed 2026-08-14.

correction_summary: Updated the clinical source from the 2017 AHRQ training module to StatPearls updated July 5, 2026, simplified overlapping distractors, and preserved the Braden-relevant risk domains.

audit_findings.claim_audit: All four risk elements in D are explicitly supported by the current source.

distractor_audit.B: Independent repositioning and adequate intake reduce the presented risk profile.
distractor_audit.C: Frequent mobility and intact sensation do not match the major risk pattern.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: D uniquely contains multiple established risk factors.
audit_findings.cueing: Options use comparable clusters rather than one disproportionately detailed key.
audit_findings.blueprint: Risk-factor recognition fits Reduction of Risk Potential.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Rechecked current Etiology and Braden sections; D remains uniquely correct.
